OK, so it seems that with this PR systemd-dissect "hangs". It might be caused by in issue in it, or it might be caused by a failure to unlock somewhere else. Either way we should figure this out before merging.

So, my educated guess is that we take the BSD lock, then release it and this means udev won't probe our loopback device if it tries to do so in this time window. Normally, it would retry it, because it watches close() events, and reprobes on each. But if we keep the fd open we just unlocked and then wait for the loopback device to be fully probed we can wait forever, since no close() is done and ths udev will not reprobe it. If you follow what I blubbering here...

I force pushed a new version that should fix that: it issues the BSD lock on a separately opened device fd. When we release the lock we also close that separate fd, which will then retrigger and we can wait for it properly. Turns out doing it like that is actually also prettier, than my earlier PR, since we can use a simple `_cleanup_close_` for automatically releasing the lock + closing the fd.
Unfortunately, TEST-50-DISSECT still hangs when waiting for the loop device.

I might have figured it out. udev watches the devices with IN_CLOSE_WRITE, hence we have to open the block device in write mode, O_RDONLY does not suffice when we are interested in udev reprobing on close().

I pushed a new version with that fixed (i.e. O_RDONLY → O_RDWR when opening the block device the second time for the BSD lock). PTAL.

So I think I tracked it down now: if a device is locked, udev won't process udev rules. The idea is to watch for IN_CLOSE_WRITE inotify events in that case, so that udev notices when the device is not used anymore and then reprobes the device. however this inotify watching is turned on by udev rules. So if we never run the rules how can this option ever be turned on?

This wasn't noticed previously I guess because we never systematically made a device pop up and immediately locked it. Because this is a race: if udev was quick enough to run its rules at least once before the device was locked the watch would be turned on, and then stayed on for good until the device went away again.

I now added a fix for this: first of all the watches are now removed again when the rules say so. Thus on each device event you can turn on/off the watching individually and it will matter until the next event is seen. Secondly, whenever we encounter the device locked we'll now install the watch immediately, so that we definitely notice when the device is closed again.

This means inotify watching is now enabled by two separate conditions: by explicit rules *or* because the device was locked when we tried to run rules for it.

Anyway, let's see if this finally fixes things.

Just a couple of questions for my own use case's benefit: I care a lot about the "happy path" at boot, with lots of single-fs images. As far as I can see, there shouldn't be any extra probing/waiting after these changes, as they mostly apply to partitioned devices. Is that right?
Also, would having lots of pre-allocated loop devices (CONFIG_BLK_DEV_LOOP_MIN_COUNT) help with avoiding the attach-empty-file-to-clean fallback? Or would it make it worse?

> Just a couple of questions for my own use case's benefit: I care a lot about the "happy path" at boot, with lots of single-fs images. As far as I can see, there shouldn't be any extra probing/waiting after these changes, as they mostly apply to partitioned devices. Is that right?

This makes no real changes what we wait for, just corrects how we do it. And while that might have worked incorrectly before for the partition sub block devices it always worked correctly for the main block device, and thus performance shouldn't have changed.

> Also, would having lots of pre-allocated loop devices (CONFIG_BLK_DEV_LOOP_MIN_COUNT) help with avoiding the attach-empty-file-to-clean fallback? Or would it make it worse?

I doubt it would change much. After all when the issue happens the device is detached and sticks around. In the bug condition it sticks around because of the kernel won#t collect it as long as the partition block devices are still around. If you pre-allocate devices, then they will also stay around otherwise, regardless of the bug or not...
